lesson.title: Molarity: Counting Moles by the Liter
lesson.summary: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution, the concentration unit built directly on the mole concept and used throughout the chemistry laboratory.
lesson.body:
Molarity, symbol M, is defined as moles of solute divided by liters of solution, not liters of solvent, a distinction that trips up nearly every student the first time around. The solvent added and the solute dissolved into it combine to some final total solution volume, and that final volume, measured after mixing, is what goes in the denominator.

Getting to molarity almost always starts with the mole concept and mole calculations covered earlier: a measured mass of solute has to be converted into moles first, using moles equals mass divided by molar mass, the same mole bridge used throughout stoichiometry. Molarity is really just that mole count divided by a volume.

Here is the full calculation worked step by step. Suppose 5.85 g of solid NaCl is dissolved and diluted with water until the total solution volume reaches exactly 500. mL (0.500 L), measured in a volumetric flask. Using rounded atomic masses (Na is about 23, Cl is about 35.5), NaCl's molar mass is about 58.5 g/mol. Moles of NaCl equals 5.85 g divided by 58.5 g/mol, which is exactly 0.100 mol. Molarity equals 0.100 mol divided by 0.500 L, which is 0.200 M. That 0.200 M solution contains 0.200 mol of dissolved NaCl in every liter of solution.

The lab technique behind that number matters as much as the arithmetic. To make it correctly, the solid is dissolved in some water first, less than the final target volume, and only once it is fully dissolved is more water added carefully up to the calibration mark on a volumetric flask. Adding exactly 500 mL of water to the solid from the start would overshoot the target, because the dissolved solute itself takes up some volume.

One more nuance worth flagging: because liquids expand slightly with temperature, a solution's volume, and therefore its molarity, can shift a little with temperature even though the moles of solute inside it never change. That is different from concentration units defined by mass, which stay fixed regardless of temperature, a distinction that becomes relevant in more precise laboratory work.
